title: Interview me into a personal operating manual
summary: Your AI interviews you, then writes a one-page manual on how to work with you that you paste into every AI you use.
saves: Replaces weeks of correcting your AI one chat at a time.
text:
You are going to interview me and then write my personal operating manual: one page that tells any AI assistant how to work with me. I will paste the result into the custom instructions or memory of every AI I use.

How to run the interview:
1. Ask me one question at a time. Wait for my answer before the next one. Keep each question short. I may answer by voice, so forgive typos and filler.
2. Cover these areas, in this order, about 25 questions in all: what I do and what I am working toward this year; how I like answers (length, tone, lists or prose, how much detail); what annoys me in AI answers; what I want you to always do and never do; how I make decisions and what I want from you when I am deciding; my schedule and energy (when I think best, when I should not be bothered); the people and projects that matter most; what I want to keep private; how I want you to handle mistakes, yours and mine.
3. After each area, say back in one sentence what you heard, and let me correct it.
4. If an answer is vague, ask one follow-up with two or three concrete options to pick from.
5. Never guess facts about me. If I skip a question, leave that part out.

Then write the manual:
- Title: "How to work with [my first name]".
- Sections: Who I am (3 lines), What I am working toward, How to answer me, Always, Never, When I am deciding, Timing, Privacy, When something goes wrong.
- Use my own words where you can. Each rule is one line. Under 450 words in all.
- End with a short version under 1,500 characters for tools with small instruction boxes.

Finally, tell me exactly where to paste it in the AI tool I name, step by step, and remind me to review it every three months.

Start now with your first question.

title: Teach me anything, with a placement test and real mastery checks
summary: A patient tutor that finds your level first, teaches one idea at a time, and proves you learned it before moving on.
saves: Replaces a semester of trial and error with a course built around you.
text:
Be my private tutor for this subject: [SUBJECT]. My goal: [WHY I WANT TO LEARN IT, OR WHAT I WANT TO BE ABLE TO DO]. Time I can give: [MINUTES PER DAY].

Step 1, placement. Give me a short placement test: 8 questions that start easy and get harder, one at a time. Do not tell me the answers yet. From my answers, tell me my level in one sentence and what I already know.

Step 2, the map. Make a learning map of 10 to 20 small skills, in the order they build on each other, starting from my level. Show it as a numbered list with one line each. Ask me if the goal and map look right before we start.

Step 3, lessons. For each skill:
- Start with a small real problem or question, before any explanation.
- Ask me one or two pointed questions that lead me toward the idea.
- Then explain it in plain words, with one everyday example, and give the proper name for it.
- Check me with 3 questions: one easy, one that applies it to something new, one that mixes it with an earlier skill.
- If I miss one, explain it a different way and ask a new question on the same point. Do not move on until I get two right in a row.

Step 4, memory. At the start of each session, quiz me on 3 earlier skills, picked from the ones I found hardest. Keep a running list of my weak spots and tell me when one becomes a strength.

Rules: one idea at a time. Short messages. Never just hand me the answer to a check question; give a hint first. Say so plainly if something I believe is wrong. If I am tired or stuck, offer a 5 minute version.

Start with the placement test.

title: Red-team my decision before I make it
summary: Your AI argues against your plan, runs a pre-mortem, checks base rates, and hands back a clear verdict and a safe first step.
saves: What a sharp advisor would charge hours for.
text:
I am about to make a decision and I want you to stress-test it. Be honest, not polite. Disagree with me where the evidence does.

The decision: [WHAT I AM DECIDING]
My current choice: [WHAT I PLAN TO DO]
What matters most to me: [MY GOALS AND LIMITS: MONEY, TIME, PEOPLE, RISK]

Do these, in order:
1. Restate the decision in one sentence and list the options, including ones I did not mention, such as waiting, doing a smaller version, or doing nothing.
2. Ask me up to 5 questions whose answers would change your view. Wait for my answers.
3. Steelman each option: the strongest honest case for it.
4. Pre-mortem: imagine it is one year later and my choice failed badly. Write the 5 most likely reasons why, most likely first.
5. Base rates: what usually happens to people who make this kind of choice? Say what you know, how sure you are, and what you do not know. Do not make up numbers.
6. Score the options in a small table: each of my goals as a row, each option as a column, a 1 to 5 score with a reason of a few words in each cell.
7. Name the one or two facts that would flip the result, and how I could check them cheaply this week.
8. Give your verdict in one sentence, your confidence, and the safest first step that keeps my options open.

Keep it tight. Plain words. No flattery.

title: Record a grandparent's life story, with the right questions
summary: Your AI guides a recorded conversation with an older relative, then turns it into a family story book and a simple family tree.
saves: Turns one afternoon into a keepsake the family keeps for generations.
text:
Help me record the life story of [NAME, MY RELATIONSHIP TO THEM, ROUGH AGE]. I will sit with them and read your questions aloud, or they will talk to you directly. Some sessions may be by phone.

Before we start:
1. Give me a short checklist: ask permission to record, pick a quiet room, test the phone recorder, bring old photos, keep sessions under 45 minutes, and plan breaks.
2. Write a warm one-paragraph opening I can read to them that explains why we are doing this.

The interview:
- Prepare 6 sessions of about 12 questions each: early childhood and parents; growing up and school; work and the world they lived through; love, family, and raising children; hard times and what got them through; beliefs, advice, and what they want remembered.
- Questions must be open and concrete ("Describe the kitchen in the house you grew up in"), never yes or no.
- After each answer I paste or type, suggest one gentle follow-up that asks for a specific moment, a name, a smell, or a place.
- If a topic is painful, offer to skip it. Never push.

After each session, from my notes or transcript:
- Write the story in their voice, in first person, keeping their phrases. Mark anything you were unsure about with [check].
- Keep a running list of names, places, and dates, and a simple family tree as an indented list.
- List 3 photos or documents to look for before the next session.

At the end, assemble a short book: title page, table of contents, one chapter per session, the family tree, and a page of their advice in their own words. Do not invent anything they did not say.

title: Set up an AI helper for an older parent
summary: Turns any AI into a patient, scam-aware helper for someone who is new to technology: large clear steps, no jargon, and a call-family rule for anything risky.
saves: Saves dozens of support calls and a lot of worry.
text:
From now on you are a patient helper for [NAME], who is [AGE RANGE] and new to computers and phones. I am setting you up for them. Follow these rules in every conversation with them.

How to talk:
- Short sentences. Plain words. No technical terms; if one is unavoidable, explain it in a few words.
- One step at a time. Number each step. Wait for them to say "done" before the next step.
- Say exactly what they will see on the screen and where: the color, the words on the button, top or bottom of the screen.
- Be warm and never rushed. If they repeat a question, answer it again kindly as if for the first time.
- If they seem confused, offer to start over with smaller steps.

Safety rules, always:
- If a message, call, email, or website asks for money, gift cards, a password, a code that was texted to them, bank details, or remote access to their computer, say clearly: "Stop. This could be a scam. Do not reply or click anything. Call [TRUSTED PERSON AND NUMBER] first."
- Never tell them to type a password or card number into a chat with you.
- If they ask about medicine, a symptom, or a legal or money decision, give general information only and suggest they ask their doctor, pharmacist, or [TRUSTED PERSON].
- If they sound upset, lonely, or unwell, be kind, and suggest calling someone they trust. If anything sounds like an emergency, tell them to call the emergency number.

What they will likely ask for help with: [LIST, FOR EXAMPLE VIDEO CALLS WITH GRANDCHILDREN, PHOTOS, EMAIL, BILLS, THE TV REMOTE].

Start by greeting [NAME] by name, saying in two sentences what you can help with, and asking what they would like to do today.

title: Is this message a scam? A careful second opinion
summary: Paste any suspicious text, email, or call script. Your AI checks it against known scam patterns and tells you what to do, without clicking anything.
saves: Takes a few minutes and can save real money.
text:
I received the message below and I am not sure it is real. Check it carefully. Do not open any links or contact anyone; only read what I pasted.

[PASTE THE MESSAGE, OR DESCRIBE THE CALL. INCLUDE THE SENDER ADDRESS OR NUMBER IF YOU HAVE IT.]

1. Give me a verdict in the first line: Likely scam, Suspicious, or Likely genuine, and how sure you are.
2. List the warning signs you see, each with the exact words from the message: urgency or threats, requests for money, gift cards, crypto, codes or passwords, a sender address or link that does not match the company, unusual payment methods, offers too good to be true, requests to keep it secret, or to move to another app.
3. List anything that looks genuine, so I get a fair picture.
4. Tell me what to do now, in numbered steps. If I need to check with the company, tell me to use the phone number or website from my own card, bill, or the company's official app, never from the message.
5. If I already clicked, replied, paid, or shared a code, tell me exactly what to do in the next hour, in order: who to call, what to change, what to watch.
6. Write a short note I can forward to my family so they can spot the same trick.

Plain words, short lines. Do not scare me more than the facts justify.

title: Explain this bill, contract, or letter line by line
summary: Paste or upload any bill, lease, contract, policy, or official letter. Get the plain-English meaning, every fee and deadline, and the questions to ask before you sign or pay.
saves: What an hour with a patient expert would give you.
text:
Read the document I am giving you and explain it to me in plain language. I am not a lawyer or accountant. Treat this as general information, not legal or financial advice, and tell me when I should ask a professional.

[PASTE THE TEXT OR ATTACH THE FILE. SAY WHAT IT IS AND WHAT I AM BEING ASKED TO DO, FOR EXAMPLE SIGN, PAY, OR RENEW.]

Give me:
1. The point in two sentences: what this is, and what it wants from me.
2. Money: every amount, fee, rate, penalty, and charge, in a table with what it is for and when it applies. Point out anything that can go up, renews by itself, or is charged later.
3. Dates: every deadline, notice period, and renewal date, soonest first.
4. My obligations and theirs, side by side.
5. Traps: clauses that are unusual, one-sided, hard to cancel, or easy to miss, with the exact words quoted and why they matter.
6. What is missing that I would expect to see.
7. Questions to ask before I sign or pay, worded so I can send them as they are.
8. A short draft reply or email if I need to dispute, cancel, or ask for changes.

Quote the exact text for every claim you make about the document. If a part is unclear or you cannot read it, say so instead of guessing.

title: A research brief that grades its own sources
summary: Your AI researches a question the way a careful analyst would: it separates strong evidence from weak, shows where sources disagree, and says what is still unknown.
saves: A day of reading, organized in minutes.
text:
Research this question for me: [QUESTION]. Why I am asking and what I will do with the answer: [CONTEXT]. If you can search the web, do; if not, say so and work only from what you know, with your knowledge cutoff stated.

Method:
1. Restate the question precisely and list the 3 to 6 sub-questions that together answer it.
2. For each sub-question, gather evidence from the strongest sources available: systematic reviews and official data first, then peer-reviewed studies, then expert bodies, then reputable journalism. Use other sources only if nothing better exists, and label them.
3. For every claim, give the source, the year, and a grade: Strong (consistent, high-quality evidence), Moderate, Weak, or Disputed.
4. Show where good sources disagree, and the most likely reason (different populations, methods, dates, or interests).
5. Separate what is known, what is likely, and what is unknown.

Deliver:
- A one-paragraph answer up top, with your confidence.
- A table of key claims: claim, grade, sources.
- What would change the answer.
- A short list of the 5 best sources to read myself, with links if you have them.

Rules: never invent a source, a quote, a number, or a link. If you are not sure a source exists, leave it out and say what kind of source would settle the point. Plain words; define any technical term once.

title: Turn a messy meeting into decisions, owners, and drafted follow-ups
summary: Paste a transcript or rough notes. Get the decisions, who owes what by when, the open questions, and ready-to-send follow-up messages.
saves: Saves the hour after every meeting.
text:
Below are the notes or transcript from a meeting. Turn them into something people can act on today.

[PASTE NOTES OR TRANSCRIPT. ADD THE MEETING TITLE, DATE, AND WHO ATTENDED IF YOU KNOW.]

Produce:
1. Summary: the purpose and the outcome in 3 lines.
2. Decisions made: each as one sentence, with who made or agreed to it. If something sounded decided but nobody said so, list it under open questions instead.
3. Action items: a table with task, owner, due date, and the exact words from the notes that support it. If the owner or date is missing, write "not stated" and do not guess.
4. Open questions and disagreements, with who raised them.
5. Risks or dependencies mentioned, and who should watch each one.
6. Follow-up messages: one short message per owner, in a friendly, direct tone, listing only their items and dates, ready to paste into email or chat. Sign them as me.
7. A suggested agenda for the next meeting, built from the open questions.

Use people's names as they appear. Keep anything sensitive (pay, health, performance, personal matters) out of the follow-up messages and flag it to me separately.

title: Build and publish your own website with your AI, step by step
summary: Your AI walks you from nothing to a live website on your own domain, using free hosting, and explains each step as you go.
saves: Days of tutorials, done in an afternoon.
text:
Help me build and publish my own simple website. I have never done this before. Go one step at a time and wait for me to say "done" after each step.

About the site: [WHAT IT IS FOR, WHO WILL VISIT, 3 THINGS IT MUST SAY OR DO]. Look and feel: [WORDS OR SITES I LIKE].

Plan to follow, unless I say otherwise:
1. Ask me 5 short questions to pin down the content. Then write all the text for a one-page site with these parts: a clear headline, what this is, why it matters, how to get in touch, and a footer. Let me edit it.
2. Build the page as one HTML file with the styles inside it. It must be fast, readable on a phone, accessible (good contrast, alt text, large tap targets), and use no tracking scripts. Show me the full file.
3. Show me how to preview it on my own computer by saving the file and opening it in my browser.
4. Publish it for free: walk me through creating a free GitHub account, a new public repository, uploading the file as index.html, and turning on GitHub Pages. Describe every button by its exact label and where it is on the screen.
5. Optional: connect my own domain. Explain what a domain is, what it usually costs per year, and how to point it at GitHub Pages, including the DNS records and turning on HTTPS.
6. Teach me how to make a change later: edit, save, upload, and check the live site.

Rules: explain each new term in one sentence. Never ask me for passwords; I will type them myself on the real websites. Before anything costs money, tell me the price and wait for my yes.

title: Learn how I write, then draft in my voice
summary: Give your AI samples of your own writing. It builds a style profile and drafts emails and messages that sound like you, not like a robot.
saves: Every future draft needs less editing.
text:
I want you to write drafts that sound like me. First learn my style from real samples, then build a style profile I can save.

Step 1. Ask me for 5 to 10 pieces of my own writing: a few emails, some text messages, and something longer if I have it. Tell me to remove anything private first.

Step 2. Analyze only what is in the samples and write my style profile:
- Greetings and sign-offs I actually use, by situation.
- Typical sentence length, paragraph length, and overall length of messages.
- Formality, warmth, humor, and how direct I am, each with a short quoted example.
- Words and phrases I use often, and ones I never use.
- Punctuation habits: exclamation marks, dashes, emoji, capitals.
- How I ask for things, how I say no, and how I apologize.
Do not invent habits that the samples do not show. Where samples disagree, say which context each belongs to.

Step 3. Test it. Draft 3 short messages in my voice: a friendly reply, a firm no, and a request to someone I do not know well. Ask me what sounds wrong, and update the profile.

Step 4. Give me the final profile in under 300 words, formatted so I can paste it into my AI's custom instructions, with this line at the top: "When drafting anything in my name, follow this style profile."

title: A 20 minute weekly review that keeps your life on track
summary: Your AI runs a calm weekly check-in: what happened, what matters next week, what to drop, and one thing to look forward to.
saves: The habit that productivity coaches charge for.
text:
Run my weekly review with me. Keep it to about 20 minutes. Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer. I may answer by voice.

1. Look back: Ask what went well this week, what did not, and what I learned. Reflect each answer back in one line.
2. Loose ends: Ask me to list everything on my mind, big or small: tasks, worries, promises I made, things I am waiting on from others. Do not judge; just collect.
3. Sort: Put each item into one of four groups and show me the result: Do next week, Schedule for later, Hand off or ask someone, Drop. Suggest a group for each and let me change it. Be honest if I am keeping too much.
4. Next week: Ask about my fixed commitments next week. Then help me choose my top 3 outcomes for the week, worded as results, not activities. Check they fit the time I actually have.
5. People: Ask who I want to reach out to this week and why. Suggest a one-line message for each.
6. Energy: Ask how I am feeling and what would make next week easier. Offer one small change, not a lecture.
7. Close: Give me a one-screen summary: top 3 outcomes, the do-next-week list, the waiting-on list, messages to send, and one thing to look forward to.

If I have a calendar, task list, or email connected, offer to read them for step 2 and 4, and ask before you change anything.

title: Turn any rough prompt into a great one
summary: Paste a prompt you use. Your AI interviews you about what you really want, then rewrites it with the structure that strong prompts share.
saves: The bar this site sets, applied to your own prompts.
text:
Help me turn a rough prompt into an excellent one. Here is my prompt:

[PASTE YOUR PROMPT]

Step 1. Diagnose. In a short list, say what is missing or unclear: the goal, who the answer is for, the context the AI needs, the steps, the format of the answer, quality checks, what to do when unsure, and limits (length, tone, things to avoid). Note anything that invites the AI to guess or make things up.

Step 2. Interview me. Ask up to 6 questions, one at a time, to fill the gaps. Offer 2 or 3 example answers with each question so I can pick quickly.

Step 3. Rewrite. Produce the improved prompt with these parts, in plain words:
- Role and goal: what the AI is doing and why.
- Context: the facts it needs, with placeholders in [BRACKETS] for anything I will fill in each time.
- Steps: numbered, in order, including when to stop and ask me.
- Output: the exact shape of the answer.
- Rules: honesty (say when unsure, never invent sources or numbers), privacy, and anything I must approve first.
- A first action, so the AI knows how to begin.

Step 4. Test. Run the new prompt once on a realistic example, show me the result, and point out one thing to tweak.

Step 5. Give me the final prompt in one copyable block, and a 2-line version for quick use.
